newsitem.title: UK: Britain expected to rule on beer merger this week.
newsitem.headline: Britain expected to rule on beer merger this week.

text.p: Britain's Department of Trade and Industry is expected to decide this week whether a proposed merger between brewer to hotels group Bass Plc and Carlsberg-Tetley should be allowed to go ahead, share analysts said on Tuesday.
"There is a market rumour that it will be this week," said Colin Davies, an analyst at Goldman Sachs.
"Everyone seems to think the 12th (of June) but we shall see," said one analyst who declined to be named. "So we will just watch our screens at eleven and three."
The traditional time for government announcements on competition issues is 1000 GMT and 1400 GMT.
"We are expecting it any day now, in fact we thought it might have been last Friday," said Shai Hill, an analyst at SocGen.
A spokesman for the ministry said, "I am not able to give a specific date because the information is market-sensitive."

Many analysts think Margaret Beckett, appointed only a month ago as Labour's trade and industry minister, will take a dim view of the proposed merger and favours tough conditions to champion the consumers' cause.
If the deal goes ahead it will create Britain's largest brewer, commanding more than 35 percent of Britain's beer market.
The Bass nshare price has slipped in recent days, falling again by some 3.5 to 742.5p on Tuesday, amid growing speculation that the decision will prove too tough for Bass to accept.
If the ruling goes against it, Bass could sell on Allied Domecq's stake in C-T to Carlsberg for 110 million pounds ($179.9 million) and Allied in turn will repay Bass 30 million.
It will mark the most important decision on competition policy since the Labour Party came to power a month ago.

Analysts think the Monopolies and Mergers Commission report, on which Beckett will base her decision, will require Bass to free its 1,500 tenanted pubs from the tie rather than require the company to sell any of its beer brands.
Brewers in Britain are allowed to operate a so-called tied system whereby the pubs they own are obliged to stock only their own beers.
Every acquisition in the beer industry since the government's Beer Orders of 1992 has required the merged group to reduce the size of its tied estate.

Approval of the deal would enable Bass, whose estimated 23 percent of the market makes it the UK's second biggest brewer, to leapfrog Scottish and Newcastle which sells 29 in every 100 pints consumed.
In the Midlands and parts of northern England, the enlarged Bass operation would supply more than 70 percent of pubs.

But Beckett may also take heed of warnings from some industry observers that more jobs will be lost if the deal is blocked. Analysts argue that once a beer supply agreement between C-T and Allied Domecq's pubs expires next March C-T's profits will slump, requiring it to offer big discounts and cut costs.
So far Beckett has referred three mergers to the MMC. Bids by National Express to run ScotRail and Central Trains were referred against the advice of the Office of Fair Trading.
She also referred the planned takeover by Charter Medical of England of Priory Hospital Group - in accordance with the OFT's advice.
Under the deal struck last August, Bass paid 200 million pounds for the 50 percent interest in C-T owned by drinks group Allied Domecq.

Carlsberg, the Danish brewer that held the rest, agreed to contribute its interest to Bass, together with 20 million pounds, in exchange for 20 percent of the merged Bass Brewers/Carlsberg-Tetley business.
($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
